final_proof:
The conclusion under the intended independent-sex model is that the two expectations are equal. Here is a precise formulation and proof.

Let the population be V={1,…,N}, with a fixed partition into nonempty families. For i∈V, let F(i) be i's family and n_i=|F(i)|. Let X_i be 1 if i is male and 0 if i is female. We interpret the assumptions as saying that P(X_i=1)=P(X_i=0)=1/2 for every i and that the variables belonging to any one family are mutually independent. No assumption about the family sizes is made. Let I be chosen uniformly from V, independently of all the sex variables, and put

B=Σ_{j∈F(I), j≠I} X_j,

the number of brothers of I. All sex assignments are retained, including assignments producing an all-male or all-female family.

First observe that, for x∈{0,1}, conditioning on X_I=x does not change the distribution of the label I. Indeed,

P(I=i | X_I=x) = [P(I=i)P(X_i=x)]/P(X_I=x) = [(1/N)(1/2)]/(1/2)=1/N.

Now fix i. If j∈F(i) and j≠i, independence within the family gives

P(X_j=1 | X_i=x)=P(X_j=1)=1/2

for both x=0 and x=1. By linearity of conditional expectation,

E(B | I=i, X_i=x)=Σ_{j∈F(i), j≠i} E(X_j | X_i=x)=(n_i−1)/2.

Consequently, by conditioning on I,

E(B | X_I=x)=Σ_{i∈V} P(I=i | X_I=x) E(B | I=i,X_i=x)
= (1/(2N)) Σ_{i∈V}(n_i−1),

and the right-hand side is independent of x. Taking x=0 and x=1 proves

E(B | I is female)=E(B | I is male).

Thus neither sex has more brothers in expectation. The unspecified family-size distribution is immaterial. The same proof also applies to random family sizes provided the family structure is independent of the sex assignments and the displayed expectation is finite.

The proposed family-by-family argument fails because it averages with different weights. In a realized family containing b boys and g girls, each girl has b brothers and each boy has b−1 brothers. But this family contributes g people to the female average and b people to the male average. Over realized families r, the two empirical averages are

A_f = [Σ_r g_r b_r]/[Σ_r g_r],   A_m = [Σ_r b_r(b_r−1)]/[Σ_r b_r].

The pointwise inequality b_r>b_r−1 compares two people in the same family, but it does not compare these two ratios, whose weights g_r and b_r differ. For a concrete refutation, take two families with (b,g)=(4,1) and (b,g)=(1,4). In each family a girl has exactly one more brother than a boy. Nevertheless there are five people of each sex, and

A_f=(1·4+4·1)/5=8/5, whereas A_m=(4·3+1·0)/5=12/5.

So even the direction of the aggregate comparison does not follow from the within-family comparison. Under the random model, all possible compositions—including the all-boy and all-girl cases that the informal comparison cannot pair—average out exactly as proved above. Equivalently, in a family of size n, there are n(n−1) ordered pairs of distinct members. Each ordered pair is (female, male) with probability 1/4 and (male, male) with probability 1/4, so the expected total number of brother-incidences credited to females and to males is n(n−1)/4 in both cases.

Finally, the phrase 'half are men and half are women' requires care. Independent fair assignments give half of the population male in expectation, not necessarily exactly in every realization. If instead one imposes exactly N/2 males by choosing uniformly among all assignments with that total, one has changed the model: the sex variables are no longer independent. In that alternative model, writing s̄=(1/N)Σ_i(n_i−1), exchangeability gives

E(B | I female)=s̄·[N/2]/(N−1),
E(B | I male)=s̄·[N/2−1]/(N−1),

so the female expectation exceeds the male expectation by s̄/(N−1). This is precisely the finite-population 'a man occupies one male slot' effect. It does not occur under the independence assumption, because there is no fixed total number of male slots. Hence, under the assumptions intended in the question—fair independent sexes—the rigorous answer is equality; a literal exact-balance constraint is a different, dependent probability model.
